text: s have thus been widely investigated and incorporated into treatment.4,5 US guidelines for colon cancer4 consider adjuvant therapy unnecessary in stage I disease, but recommend adjuvant chemotherapy in most patients with resectable stage II or stage III disease. There is good evidence that fluorouracil-based adjuvant therapy improves survival in stage III disease,6-10 and it has been regarded as the standard of care.2,9,11,12 Recent results with the FOLFOX regimen (infusional fluorour- acil, folinic acid, and oxaliplatin) have suggested that it can improve disease-free (but not overall) survival in this group.13 Oral fluoropyrimidines have also been shown to improve survival after resection;14 guidelines suggest that intravenous fluorouracil plus folinic acid, FOLFOX, or oral capecitabine are all suitable adjuvant regimens.4 Re- sults with the IFL regimen, which adds irinotecan to bolus fluorouracil and folinic acid, have not proved satisfactory because of its toxicity,2,10,12 and FOLFIRI (infusional fluorouracil with folinic acid and irinotecan) has not been shown to be superior to fluorouracil/folinic acid in the ad- juvant setting.4 In contrast, the evidence in favour of adjuvant therapy in patients with stage II colon cancer is much weaker:12,15 US guidelines recommend its consideration, particularly in patients with poor prognostic features and within the con- text of a clinical study,4 but its routine use is not advised:16 such therapy would not improve survival by more than 5%. Neoadjuvant therapy and radiotherapy seem to play little role in the management of early colon cancer, and the latter is not generally recommended,2 although it may be consid- ered where there is tumour penetration of fixed structures.4 In contrast, in the management of early stage rectal cancer they play an important role. Local recurrence is common with rectal cancer, and radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy can help reduce this. US guidelines suggest that surgery alone may be considered in patients with stage I disease.5 Traditionally, adjuvant chemoradiotherapy was consid- ered the standard of care for patients with stage II or stage III rectal cancer, but more recently neoadjuvant (pre-oper- ative) treatment has been advocated on the basis of better local tumour control and lower morbidity:2 it decreases tu- mour volume and thus enhances sphincter preservation.5 A meta-analysis17 found that adjuvant radiotherapy re- duced the risk of local recurrence; the risk of death from rectal cancer may have been reduced, particularly for pre- operative radiotherapy but there was little impact on over- all survival. A subsequent large randomised study also found that pre-operative chemoradiotherapy (fluorouracil infusion plus fractionated pelvic radiotherapy) improved local control and was associated with less toxicity than postoperative treatment, but did not improve overall sur- vival.
